problems.title: Fair walk
problems.statement: A simple random walk from 0 stops at +3 or −7.

problems.title: Martingale?
problems.statement: Which are martingales for a fair ±1 walk Sₙ?
problems.solution: Sₙ² drifts up by 1 per step; 2^{Sₙ} drifts up too (E[2^X] = 5/4).

problems.title: Doubling with a bankroll
problems.statement: Double after each loss on a fair coin; you can afford at most 10 consecutive losses (bankroll $1,023).

parts.prompt: P(losing the whole bankroll in a round)?

problems.title: Roulette
problems.statement: Bet red at p = 18/38, $1 per spin, start at $50, stop at $100 or $0.
problems.solution: Only ≈ 0.0051 with $1 bets. In an unfavourable game, bold play (few large bets) maximises your chance of hitting a target.

problems.title: Ballot
problems.statement: Candidate A gets 6 votes and B gets 4, counted in random order.

parts.prompt: P(A strictly ahead throughout the count)?

problems.title: Wald
problems.statement: Roll a die repeatedly until the running total is at least 100.

parts.prompt: Approximate expected number of rolls (100/3.5 plus overshoot ≈ 5/3 ÷ 3.5)?

hints: E[S_τ] = E[τ]·3.5; the expected overshoot ≈ (E[X²]/(2E[X])) − ½ ≈ 5/3.

problems.title: Exponential martingale
problems.statement: A biased walk with p = 2/3 up, q = 1/3 down.
hints: Let N → ∞ in the ruin formula.
problems.solution: (q/p)^{Sₙ} is a martingale; the probability of ever dropping by k is (q/p)ᵏ = 2⁻ᵏ.

problems.title: Stopping when ahead
problems.statement: A fair walk from 0, stop the first time you're at +1 (no bankroll limit).

options: No: S_τ = 1 always; optional stopping fails because E[τ] = ∞

problems.solution: The walk hits +1 with probability 1, but the expected time is infinite and the losses before stopping are unbounded.
